extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / general literate public interested in moral and social essays
extracted.subtask_description: Short, periodical moral and humorous essays (The Spectator style) that mix satire, anecdote, and practical moral advice for a general eighteenth‑century readership. The pieces comment on manners, writing, conduct, and useful occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Itch of Writing (Cacoethes) — remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an epidemic 'Itch of Writing' (Cacoethes); some cures (satyrs, lampoons) fail; the only effectual cure is to forbid the patient the use of pen, ink, and paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failed 'remedies' (satyrs, lampoons, pillory) are given; a cat-call (public jeer) sometimes checks it but the sure cure is prohibition of writing materials. This is both a diagnosis of a literary malady and a prescriptive remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the endlessness of periodical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodical writers whose works return on stated days are 'more offensive, and more incurable' because their labours never come to an end and the reader cannot rely on ever reaching a conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: producing never‑ending serials that demand perpetual reader patience. Implicit criterion for good periodical practice: provide satisfaction or closure rather than endlessly extending content merely to fill dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the press to convey truth and knowledge, not prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of printing should be a great blessing to mankind, not an instrument to scatter prejudice and ignorance among the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers/publishers are counseled to avoid spreading falsehoods or prejudices; the medium's moral duty is to promote truth and knowledge. Printing used otherwise is a perversion of its potential benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers should illuminate, not darken (be 'stars that scatter light')
rubrics_metrics.description: Some writers are like heavenly stars that scatter light, others are 'tenebrificous' and ray out darkness — good writing should enlighten its readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation: identify whether an author clarifies and enlightens (positive) or obscures and misleads (negative). The essayist promises to 'rise upon' and dispel the 'dark' writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer durable, improving works (the virtue of planting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Planting (literally) is presented as an employment that gives pleasure of a more lasting date and continually improves; contrasted with buildings which decay once finished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a general standard for laudable enterprises: choose projects that yield ongoing improvement and lasting public benefit. Metaphorically applicable to literary or civic projects—value permanence and progressive improvement over ephemeral display.

rubrics_metrics.name: All should fix on useful employments; avoid idleness
rubrics_metrics.description: No one ought to think himself exempt from labour and industry; those with birth or fortune must still find a calling so as not to be burdensome to the species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral criterion for personal conduct: seek occupations useful to yourself or beneficial to others. Anti-pattern: living idly on fortune without contributing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small public‑minded acts (for posterity) are morally significant
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting a few twigs into the ground can benefit posterity fifty years hence; failing to do such small good works indicates a poor and base heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of civic virtue: willingness to perform small, long‑term beneficent acts is a sign of generosity and love for mankind. Encourages modest but enduring contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select useful offices suited to modest talents
rubrics_metrics.description: Many honest minds feel they lack talents for great good, but planting (and similar offices) is suited even to the meanest capacities and can be performed by multitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for social usefulness: one need not be a genius to deserve well of the country; perform modest, practical services rather than despairing of contributing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planting (or analogous pursuits) composes the mind and engenders good thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: Amusements like planting are not tumultuous pleasures but lasting, they compose the mind, quiet passions, and engender laudable contemplations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a standard for wholesome occupations: prefer those that calm the soul and produce moral reflection rather than excite transient passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dreams for self‑examination and improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow Pythagoras: examine nightly what you have done that day and in the morning consider what occurred in your sleep; dreams arise from waking thoughts and reveal inclinations to be checked or cultivated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: nightly and morning scrutiny of dreams helps discover habits to pursue or vices to prevent. Use dream content as evidence of temper and inclinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go to bed sober and calm to cultivate wholesome dreams
rubrics_metrics.description: One maxim: 'To go to Bed with a Mind entirely free from Passion, and a Body clear of the least Intemperance' — such a habit yields beneficial and noble dreams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: sleeping after intemperance (food or drink) leads to guilty or disquieting dreams. Controlling appetite and passions before sleep is recommended to shape productive imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental rehearsal before sleep aids waking performance
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have business of consequence tomorrow, begin it in your thoughts before sleep; you may wake having rehearsed its process and thereby gain advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical technique: vividly imagine and run through tomorrow's affairs at night to gain an experiential head‑start and improve conduct on waking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge others until you have purified and examined yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you can rightly animadvert on the failings of others, you must be pure yourself — the vision of hearts in phials is introduced only after the dreamer is cut open and purified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical rule: self‑examination and correction are prerequisites for fair criticism of others. The narrative models purification as literalized in the dream.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose character by observable moral 'spots' (fomes) in the heart
rubrics_metrics.description: In the vision hearts are shown with a 'fomes' or spot whose size and colour indicate vices: a red fiery spot with agitation (ambitious restlessness), a black spot spreading (avarice/ melancholy), a small speck (vanity), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral‑psychological diagnostic: use vivid imagery of 'spots' to identify predominant faults (ambition, avarice, vanity, rancour). Examples given: Tom Dread‑Nought (ambition), Dick Gloomy (avarice/melancholy), Will Worthy (noble with vanity speck).
